clinical_knowledge.topic: Chronic Insomnia Disorder evaluation and management
core_concepts: Chronic insomnia disorder requires persistent sleep difficulty despite adequate opportunity and associated daytime impairment.
Assess sleep schedule, depression, anxiety, mania, substance use, medicines, sleep apnoea, restless legs syndrome, and circadian disturbance.
CBT-I is first-line; use a sleep diary and address conditioned wakefulness and clock-watching.
Any sedative-hypnotic requires individualized risk review, short duration, and monitoring for sedation, falls, interactions, and dependence.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: difficulty falling asleep taking over 2 hours every night with daytime fatigue

Key HPI features: 46F reports 6 months of severe conditioned insomnia. Takes over 2 hours to fall asleep at night, waking up multiple times and lying awake clock-watching. Suffers from daytime fatigue.
Objective/Exam findings: Complete vital signs and focused physical examination required. Diagnostic workup tailored for Chronic Insomnia Disorder.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Chronic Insomnia Disorder.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Adjustment disorder without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Acute suicidal or homicidal ideation.
management_principles: Offer CBT-I including stimulus control, sleep scheduling, and cognitive strategies.
Address medical, psychiatric, and substance-related contributors.
Avoid routine long-term sedative-hypnotics and urgently assess suicidality, mania, psychosis, or unsafe impairment such as drowsy driving.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

history.answer: I have been having terrible trouble falling asleep at night for the past six months. It takes me over two hours to nod off, and I feel completely exhausted during the day.
My main struggle is falling asleep initially, taking over two hours every night. Once I finally do, I wake up three or four times and lie awake for long stretches.
It started about six months ago and happens almost every single night, at least six nights a week. It has been going on continuously without a break.
It began around the start of the school semester when I took on a demanding new curriculum. The initial work stress eased up, but my sleep trouble stayed behind.

I get into bed at eleven, but I toss and turn until after one in the morning before drifting off. My alarm goes off at six-thirty, and on weekends I try to sleep in until eight, but I still cannot fall asleep easily.
I feel exhausted and drained all day, and it is hard to focus while grading papers and teaching. I have never nodded off while driving, though.
I avoid daytime naps because I want to be tired at night. Once in bed, I catch myself browsing my phone and constantly checking the clock, panicking about how few hours of rest I have left.
I drink one cup of black coffee at seven in the morning and never touch caffeine after noon. I do not drink alcohol to help me fall asleep, and I do not smoke.
My husband says I do not snore loudly, and he has never seen me stop breathing or gasp for air. I do not wake up with morning headaches or a dry mouth.
No, my legs feel completely normal at night. I do not get any creeping, crawling sensations or any urge to move them.
I work steady daytime hours as a high school English teacher. My work hours are predictable, with no night shifts or rotating schedules.
I do not feel depressed or hopeless, and I still love spending time with my family and reading. My anxiety is really centered on whether I will be able to fall asleep each night.
No, I have never had thoughts of wanting to die or harming myself. I just want to get my sleep back.
No, I have never had periods where I felt euphoric, hyperactive, or full of energy on minimal sleep. When I miss sleep, I feel utterly wiped out.
No chronic pain, no need to get up to urinate at night, and no heartburn. I also do not experience cough, breathlessness, or heart racing in bed.
I tried over-the-counter sleep aids with diphenhydramine a couple of times, but they only left me groggy the next morning. Other than my blood pressure pill, I do not take other medications.
Our bedroom is cool, quiet, and dark with blackout curtains. I share the bed with my husband, and he sleeps soundly without disturbing me.
I feel like my internal sleep clock is completely broken, and my brain has forgotten how to fall asleep naturally.
I am really worried about getting hooked on prescription sleeping pills if I start taking them. I do not want to depend on medication forever.
I am hoping to get guidance on sleep therapy and learn practical techniques to retrain my sleep habits, and perhaps discuss safe medical options.
I was diagnosed with high blood pressure three years ago, which has been well controlled. I have no other medical conditions.
I had an appendectomy when I was twenty-two, which went smoothly without complications. I have never had any other surgeries or hospital admissions.
I take lisinopril ten milligrams once a day every morning for my blood pressure. I also take a daily multivitamin.
I do not have any known allergies to medications, foods, or environmental triggers.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used electronic cigarettes in my life.
I only have a glass of wine on occasional social gatherings on weekends, maybe twice a month. I never use alcohol to help me fall asleep.
I work full-time as a high school English teacher and live in a quiet apartment with my husband. We have no children living at home.
My mother has hypertension, and my father passed away from a heart attack in his seventies. There is no family history of psychiatric illnesses or chronic sleep disorders.
My last menstrual period started two weeks ago, and my cycles come regularly every twenty-eight days with normal flow.
My husband had a vasectomy several years ago, so there is no chance of pregnancy.

Oropharynx is clear without tonsillar enlargement, Mallampati class I airway with no posterior pharyngeal crowding.
Thyroid gland is normal in size, non-tender, symmetric, and without palpable nodules or bruits.
Regular rate and rhythm with normal S1 and S2; no murmurs, gallops, or friction rubs.
Clear breath sounds throughout both lung fields without wheezing, crackles, or rhonchi.
Alert and oriented to person, place, and time; mildly anxious regarding her sleep, but affect is reactive with normal thought process and no suicidal or psychotic thoughts.
